content: 1. Infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) should receive the same general medical care as older infants with SAM. This includes the administration of parenteral antibiotics to treat potential sepsis and appropriate treatment for other medical complications such as tuberculosis (TB), HIV, surgical conditions, or disabilities. For those not admitted to inpatient care, a course of weight-adjusted broad-spectrum oral antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, should be provided. 2. Feeding strategies for infants under six months with SAM should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding by the mother or caregiver. If breastfeeding is not possible, support should be provided to help the mother or caregiver relactate. If relactation is not feasible, wet-nursing should be encouraged. Supplementary feeding approaches, such as expressed breast milk, commercial infant formula, or specialized therapeutic feeds like F-75 or diluted F-100, may be used as needed. Undiluted F-100 should never be given due to the risk of hypernatremic dehydration. 3. The physical and mental health of mothers or caregivers should be assessed, and appropriate treatment or support should be provided to address any identified issues. 4. Infants admitted to inpatient care can be transferred to outpatient care when all clinical conditions, including edema, are resolved, the infant has a good appetite, is clinically well and alert, and demonstrates adequate weight gain. Immunizations and routine interventions should be up to date, and caregivers should be linked to community-based follow-up and support. 5. Infants can be discharged from all care when they are effectively breastfeeding or feeding well with replacement feeds, have adequate weight gain, and achieve a weight-for-length z-score of -2 or higher. 6. For children aged 6–59 months with moderate acute malnutrition, management should include breastfeeding promotion, family education, and nutrition counseling. Interventions to address underlying causes of malnutrition, such as food insecurity, should also be implemented. Nutrient-dense foods should be provided to meet their additional needs for weight and height gain and functional recovery. 7. For HIV-exposed infants, nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be considered to identify HIV infection. Point-of-care NAT technologies and rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV serology can be used for early infant diagnosis. RDTs can also be used to rule out HIV infection in asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants at nine months of age and to diagnose HIV in children older than 18 months following national testing strategies. 8. Provider-initiated HIV testing and counseling should be routinely offered to infants and children with unknown HIV status in generalized epidemic settings, particularly those admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics. Adolescents should also be offered HIV testing and counseling, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care services. 9. Adolescents living with HIV should be counseled on the benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status and supported in determining if, when, how, and to whom to disclose. Community-based approaches and healthcare worker training can improve treatment adherence and retention in care. 10. ART should be initiated in all children living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, with priority given to infants diagnosed in the first year of life and children under two years of age. For adolescents, ART should also be initiated regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, with priority for those with severe or advanced HIV disease. 11. For children and adolescents with TB and HIV, ART should be started as soon as possible within the first eight weeks of TB treatment, and within the first two weeks for those with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³. 12. First-line ART regimens for adolescents should include two NRTIs plus an NNRTI or an INSTI, with TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + EFV as the preferred option. Alternative regimens may be used if the preferred options are contraindicated or unavailable. 13. For children aged three to ten years, the NRTI backbone for ART should include ABC + 3TC or AZT/TDF + 3TC (or FTC). For children under three years, the NRTI backbone should include ABC or AZT + 3TC. 14. Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at six months, 12 months, and then annually for patients stable on ART. CD4 cell count monitoring can be stopped in individuals who are stable on ART and virally suppressed. 15. Dried blood spot specimens can be used to determine HIV viral load, with a threshold of 1,000 copies/mL used to define virological failure. 16. After failure of a first-line LPV/r-based regimen, children under three years should switch to a RAL-based second-line regimen. Older children should switch to a second-line regimen containing two NRTIs plus EFV or RAL. After failure of a first-line NNRTI-based regimen, children should switch to a boosted PI-based regimen, with LPV/r or ATV/r as preferred options.
